#5107. CFTC approves individual stock perpetual futures trading in US for the first time

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

Perpetual futures contracts surged in popularity over the past year, particularly after disruptions in global supply chains in the Middle East earlier this year at the onset of the war.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission approved the ability for exchanges in the United States to offer perpetual futures contracts tied to individual stocks — just months after those assets were put into the spotlight by President Donald Trump.

On Tuesday, CFTC Chair Michael Selig greenlit the ability to trade those perpetual futures contracts for the first time in the U.S. for platforms.

"This expansion marks a significant step towards allowing U.S. market participants, consistent with applicable law, to avail themselves of the advantages of perpetual futures that have led to their emergence as widely sought tools for risk-management and price-discovery," Selig said.

Perpetuals, or perps, are a type of futures contract that don't have an expiration date and allow people to bet on the price movement of assets without owning them directly.

Perpetual futures contracts surged in popularity over the past year, particularly after disruptions in global supply chains in the Middle East earlier this year at the onset of the war, after the U.S. and Israel conducted missile strikes on Iran, which triggered supply shocks. That happened over the weekend, so traditional oil futures markets were closed, but platforms like Hyperliquid operate 24/7, so much of the trading happened onchain.

Over the past year, the CFTC has approved a few perpetual futures contracts. The agency first opened the door for bitcoin perpetual futures contracts in the U.S. when its staff greenlit KalshiEX and Coinbase to list the products. Then in June, the CFTC released a request for comment on crude oil perpetual contracts and 24/7 trading.

Perpetuals futures contracts have also caught Trump's attention. In August, he said he wanted the CFTC to work to bring Hyperliquid into the U.S.

Both the SEC and CFTC would oversee the contracts, Selig said on Tuesday.

"This framework recognized the complementary roles of the CFTC and SEC in overseeing American financial markets by providing a pathway for innovation at the intersection of the U.S.," Selig said.

#5106. What Is The Bare Minimum Amount Of Strength Training You Need To Do For It To Be Effective? Here's What Trainers Say

Right up there with a balanced diet, strength training is the OG biohack for longevity, and the key to a strong, healthy body. But whether you’re a beginner or seasoned athlete, that begs the question: How much strength training do you actually need to see results?

If you look to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for answers, they say that adults need at least two days of “muscle-strengthening activity" per week for their overall health. But, resistance training even once a week was enough to make progress for beginners, per a study in BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation.

"While it may seem the small amount of volume would be insignificant, this study demonstrates that some exercise is better than no exercise,” says certified personal trainer Natalya Vasquez. But as your skill level progresses, you’ll need to increase the intensity and volume of your workouts to elicit more muscle growth.

Below, experts explain exactly how much strength training is enough based on your fitness level and goals.

Meet the experts: Tina Tang, CPT, is a certified personal trainer, strength coach, and founder of Iron Strong Fitness. Natalya Vasquez, CPT, is a certified personal trainer, health coach, and founder of On Your Terms Coaching.

The following cheat-sheet will give you an idea of how many days a week you should strength train.

While once a week was enough for the folks in the aforementioned study to make progress, they only looked at a single exercise: the leg press. Vasquez says that ideally, beginners looking to build total-body muscle and strength should start with two, or even three, nonconsecutive strength training sessions per week.

This frequency helps build a habit (key for those just starting out) and provides your body with the necessary stimulus for initial muscle growth, while also allowing for plenty of time to recover. But, your sessions don't have to be long: Initially, each session can be as short as 15 to 20 minutes, and you can gradually increase to 45- to 60-minute workouts as you build endurance, says certified personal trainer Tina Tang, CPT.

As for how you structure your workouts, Vasquez says you can either do two to three full-body workouts, or a three-day split, like a push/pull/legs workout, where your training is organized by muscle group.

For a full-body routine, Vasquez suggests completing one exercise per muscle group for three to five sets of five to eight reps per workout. For a three-day split, complete three to four exercises for the same muscle group for two to three sets of five to eight reps.

Vasquez likes the five to eight rep range because she says this helps develop functional hypertrophy: “We don’t just want to gain muscle, we want to have actual strength where this muscle growth is functional,” she says.

“You don’t need complicated gym equipment to get results,” says Vasquez. “Dumbbells and bands are affordable, convenient, and versatile options for exercising at home, and as your strength increases, gym access may be beneficial since it’ll give you additional equipment and a wider selection of weights.”

In this case, the trainers suggest strength training three times a week, and depending on the intensity and volume of the workout, each session should range between 30 to 60 minutes, Tang says. “This frequency is effective for preserving muscle mass and strength while ensuring adequate recovery and adaptation.”

However, overall volume may be more important that days per week, according to a 2021 review in Sports Medicine. The researchers conclude that it's possible to see gains by training anywhere from one to four days per week so long as you're getting in at least four sets of six to 15 reps per muscle group per week.

The key here will be to follow the principle of progressive overload. Gradually increasing the weight, sets and or reps, over time will continually challenge the muscles, stimulate growth, and improve bone density, says Tang. “The body craves movement, and once it's accustomed to a certain level of activity, it needs more of a challenge to keep making gains."

Good news: The longer you’ve been strength training, the less work you’ll need to maintain your gains since your muscles are composed of more fibers, says Vasquez. “So if you’ve been strength training five times per week for a decade and then something happens in your life that doesn’t allow you to work out as much, you’ll still be able to maintain your muscle with one full-body workout per week,” she says. However, this would be the bare minimum, and resistance training two to three times a week is still the ideal sweet spot.

In terms of the type of training, Tang also recommends full-body workouts to maintain balanced muscle development and overall strength. Look to hit all the major movement patterns for best results. For each exercise, Vasquez says to aim to complete three to five sets of five to eight reps.

Aside from logging miles, strength training at least twice a week is a crucial part of every running regimen, says Tang. “Ideally, one session can focus on bilateral, foundational movements, while a second session allows for a more specialized approach, targeting unilateral exercises, core stability, and hip strength,” she explains. “This balance ensures you're not only building overall strength but also addressing the specific needs that support running performance and injury prevention.”

Indeed, the addition of two to four strength training sessions a week helped mid- to long-distance runners prevent injury and run faster, according to a 2024 meta-analysis in the journal Sports Medicine.

Workouts should range between 30 to 60 minutes and rep ranges can vary from five to eight (with heavier weight and for more advanced strength trainers) to 12 to 20 reps (for runners newer to strength training and using lighter weights), Vasquez says.

FWIW, the meta-analysis notes that plyometric training and "high load" strength training (using weights at 80% of your one rep max or heavier), specifically, improved running economy.

For this goal, Tang says to strength train at least twice a week. Doing so "helps build and maintain muscle mass and bone density, which is crucial for protecting bones and joints as we age, and this frequency provides a balance between stimulating the muscles and allowing for adequate recovery,” she says.

Plus, regular resistance training helps strengthen tendons and ligaments, in turn, supporting joint stability and overall musculoskeletal health, she adds.

Full-body workouts and compound exercises like deadlifts, overhead presses, and squats are ideal since they involve multiple joints and mimic how your body moves in real life, says Vasquez. Depending on your experience, this could look like choosing two to three exercises and doing three to five sets for five to eight reps (to focus on building functional strength) per workout.

No matter your goals, strength training is certainly worth your time. Aside from supporting your overall wellbeing, picking up weights can prevent injury, improve metabolic health, reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease, and support bone density, especially in women, says Vasquez.

In fact, approximately one in five women over age 50 have osteoporosis (a condition that causes bones to become weak and brittle), but strength training can help enhance bone density and reduce the risk of fractures, says Tang.

Sarcopenia, an age-related progressive loss of muscle mass strength, is another common condition among women, and after age 30, you can gradually begin losing muscle mass each decade. Fortunately, strength training can again help combat the effects and reverse muscle loss, says Tang.

Finally, regular weight training supports balance, mobility, and functional strength which are crucial for performing daily activities and living independently, Tang says. “Strength training acts as an investment in our future health, ensuring that we maintain physical strength and resilience for the long term.”

Andi Breitowich is a freelance writer who covers health, fitness, relationships, beauty, and smart living. She is a graduate of Emory University and Northwestern University's Medill School of Journalism. #5105. North Korea Is Laundering Binance Hack Loot at One New Wallet Every 25 Seconds

North Korea Is Laundering Binance Hack Loot at One New Wallet Every 25 Seconds

North Korean hackers are moving the $6.4 billion they stole from Binance at a blistering clip: roughly one new crypto wallet every 25 seconds.

In under four days, the attacker has spread the funds across about 12,000 wallets on 11 blockchains in more than 40,000 transactions, according to an analysis published Monday by blockchain analytics firm Elliptic.

But stablecoin issuers moved even faster. About $2.85 billion, or 44% of the haul, has been frozen or seized, compared with roughly 3% after North Korea’s $1.5 billion hack of Bybit in February 2025.

Speed mattered because stablecoins made up $3.46 billion, or 54%, of the haul, and their issuers can freeze them. Tether froze the stolen USDT on Ethereum 37 minutes after it reached the attacker’s wallet, and Circle froze all $823 million in stolen USDC before any of it could be swapped, Elliptic found.

Before the freezes landed, the hacker swapped 434 million USDT for ETH on decentralized exchanges such as Uniswap, borrowed 19,762 ETH on lending protocol Aave against another 59.9 million USDT, and traded 234 million USDT for Tron’s TRX token. In all, about $786 million in stablecoins got away.

Attackers began draining Binance’s hot wallets late Thursday. The FBI has since attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-linked hacking group, and published hundreds of linked addresses.

Binance, which has pledged to cover all losses, reopened withdrawals Sunday and saw about $3.64 billion in net outflows in the first nine and a half hours.

The laundering that followed has been relentless. On Tron, which became the main route, activity peaked at about 1,300 transactions in a single hour.

That pace fueled speculation that AI agents were doing the work. Elliptic disagreed, pointing to fixed timing, set amounts, blind retries and pauses that resemble human working hours. The firm wrote that while the laundering is clearly automated, “nothing we have seen shows an AI agent making decisions.”

About $3.24 billion remains in addresses linked to the theft, mostly ETH and the 18,270 stolen Bitcoin, which haven’t moved since the day of the attack. Elliptic believes those funds are very likely still held by North Korea, while money already being laundered may have passed to Chinese money-laundering networks.

Only a negligible amount appears to have been cashed out. About $16 million has also flowed to addresses holding proceeds of September’s Bitget exploit.

Based on the Bybit playbook, Elliptic expects the attacker to swap its ETH for Bitcoin in small batches and cash out through over-the-counter brokers over a period of months. Further freezes will be harder, the firm said, since ETH and Bitcoin can’t be frozen. The best remaining chances lie with centralized services, where the funds will eventually have to surface.

The Binance theft caps a punishing stretch for crypto security. BTCPay Server urged merchants to switch off their servers amid reports of hot wallet attacks on Monday, and Brazilian exchange Mercado Bitcoin halted withdrawals after a $40 million hack. It’s unclear whether either incident is connected to the Binance attack.

#5100. Tom Lee Calls Bottom on AI Stock Selloff, Citing Tight Supply and Crypto Resilience

Tom Lee Calls Bottom on AI Stock Selloff, Citing Tight Supply and Crypto Resilience

Fundstrat co-founder and Bitmine chairman Tom Lee says the AI stock selloff has reached its bottom, arguing that demand remains constrained by supply and that crypto’s response to a multibillion-dollar hack suggests investors have already done much of their selling.

“I think we're at the bottom,” Lee said in a CNBC interview on Squawk Box. His call follows a decline that has spread beyond individual AI companies: large technology stocks also sit inside the funds many people use to invest for retirement. (Disclosure: Tom Lee is one of several investors in Dastan, Decrypt’s parent company.)

Lee acknowledged how difficult it is to identify the point where prices stop falling. “Bottoms are dangerous because you don't know how much more downside you have at the bottom,” he said.

His case rests on a distinction between an industry struggling to expand fast enough and one that has built more capacity than customers need.

“The market for AI is still very tight. It's not an overcapacity market,” Lee said. Constraints on spending, including political opposition, are slowing growth without signaling that the boom has peaked, he argued.

The distinction matters for companies building the infrastructure behind AI, including data centers, the facilities that house the computers running these systems. A shortage can leave customers waiting, but it can also prevent suppliers from turning orders into revenue.

Intel offered a particularly sharp example on Friday, when its shares plunged nearly 30% to $65.76 after a disappointing fourth-quarter forecast. Its data center and AI revenue had risen 78% from a year earlier to $7.3 billion, yet manufacturing constraints limited its ability to meet demand.

Intel projected quarterly revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, with the midpoint about $1.6 billion below analysts’ expectations. Its weaker PC business added pressure, showing why healthy AI demand can coexist with a falling share price.

Lee’s second argument looks outside the stock market. He pointed to crypto’s relatively limited response to the Binance security breach, which the exchange initially estimated had an impact of about $6.3 billion.

“If crypto is a leading indicator for risk, you've already seen people sort of washed out,” he said. In his reading, a market that absorbs bad news without a much larger decline may have fewer sellers left to push prices down.

Bitcoin did fall about 4% to roughly $76,400 on Friday, and more than $1.3 billion in positions funded with borrowed money were forcibly closed. U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which hold Bitcoin and trade like stocks, also shed $643.2 million that day, their largest daily outflow of October.

That said, a 4% drop can happen even during bull runs and it is considered a relatively normal occurrence among crypto traders.

Binance said on Friday that about $3 billion of the affected assets had been frozen and pledged to cover losses using its emergency reserve and company funds.

#5096. Why Am I Always So Tired? 15 Reasons You May Have Fatigue

Allergies, stress, and sugar could all play a part in your energy levels.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

The most relatable statement of all time: “I’m exhausted.” Life is stressful, busy, and often feels like an impossible balancing act. Beyond the demands of endless work tasks and social obligations, legit health reasons could explain lingering fatigue. If you’re chugging coffee on the regular and still wondering, Why am I so tired? it's worth considering whether something in your body is causing your low energy.

Obviously, if you stay up binging a new series or push yourself harder than usual while training for an upcoming race, you’re gonna feel sluggish the next day. But there’s a difference between feeling tapped out sometimes and long bouts of fatigue that won’t go away.

Meet the experts: Antoinette LaDawn Price, MD, MPH, is a family medicine doctor at Emory Physician Group Practice; Purvi Parikh, MD, is an allergist and immunologist with Allergy & Asthma Network; Sobia Khan, MD, is the director of Women's Center for Comprehensive Care at Baylor College of Medicine; Jessica Cording, RD, is the author of The Little Book of Game-Changers; Monifa Seawell, MD, is a board-certified psychiatrist in Atlanta, Georgia

“Fatigue is chronic extreme tiredness,” says Antoinette LaDawn Price, MD, MPH, at Emory Physician Group Practice. Fatigue can show up as headaches, dizziness, and achy and sore muscles, irritability, brain fog, and moodiness; it manifests differently in each person.

If you always feel drained, it may be time for you to consult your doctor about your symptoms. If you feel like something is off, don’t ignore it—there are many health issues, both mental and physical, that can make it difficult for you to last through the entire day without wanting to collapse in bed. Here are possible causes of fatigue, according to doctors.

Classic symptoms of seasonal allergies include sneezing and having watery eyes. Less common symptoms include low energy and fatigue. “If left untreated, seasonal allergies can cause fatigue,” says Purvi Parikh, MD, an allergist and immunologist with Allergy & Asthma Network. Why? Your body works hard to fend off the allergen, and that takes extra energy. That’s true whether you're allergic to outdoor triggers like ragweed or pollen, or to indoor allergens like dust mites, Dr. Parikh says.

Allergens aren’t the only things that can trigger fatigue—allergy medications can, too. “Some of the over-the-counter allergy pills like antihistamines unfortunately cause fatigue as well,” says Dr. Parikh.

How to fix it: If allergies leave you feeling completely spent, your current treatment plan may not be working. So, check in with your doctor about your options. They’ll likely recommend medication (or a different one) to help get things under control. Running a HEPA air purifier at home can also help clear the air, notes Dr. Parikh.

While going hard during your at-home workouts can wear you out, the opposite can do the same. “The human body gets more tired with progressive sedentary habits due to generalized reconditioning of the body and, ultimately, muscle loss,” explains Sobia Khan, MD, an assistant professor of general internal medicine and the director of Women's Center for Comprehensive Care at Baylor College of Medicine.

Basically, your body takes a “use it or lose it” approach to fitness. If you don’t exercise regularly, you’ll feel more tired when you start moving and even when you’re at rest.

How to fix it: This solution is pretty simple—get moving more. Just a reminder, the general physical activity recommendation is 150 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise each week, plus muscle-strengthening activity at least two days a week. Once you start moving again, it’ll be easier to get through your day-to-day stuff without being a zombie.

When you eat sugary foods or foods high in refined carbs (think: white bread, pasta, pastries), your blood sugar spikes, according to Jessica Cording, RD, author of The Little Book of Game-Changers. In the moment, that can make you feel kinda hyper. But unfortunately, you're also in for an inevitable crash, which can leave you feeling totally wiped.

If you keep overloading on sugar and refined carbs, you may also develop insulin resistance, Dr. Khan adds. That is when your body can’t use glucose (a.k.a. sugar) as well as it should for energy.

How to fix it: Cording says to cut back on sugar and refined carbs regularly. FWIW, the CDC recommends limiting added sugar to less than 10 percent of your total daily calories. (So, if you eat a 2,000-calorie diet, no more than 200 of those calories should come from added sugars.)

When you’re having sugary or carb-heavy foods, balance the meal with protein and fat, like adding nut butter to your crackers. This can help lower the odds that you’ll crash afterward, Cording says.

Stress isn’t just mental—it can affect you physically, too. “Your mind and body are closely linked and are in constant communication with one another,” says Monifa Seawell, MD, a board-certified psychiatrist in Atlanta, Georgia. “When there is a shift in your emotional state, be it positive or negative, it is not at all uncommon for that change to also show up in some physical way in your body.”

You can start getting headaches, an upset stomach, and, yep, fatigue, Dr. Seawell says.

How to fix it: The best approach is to address the root of your stress. While some stressors are unavoidable, doing your utmost to limit the ones you can address can be helpful.

Dr. Seawell also recommends scheduling 20 to 30 minutes of exercise each day. She says this can often boost your energy levels when you can’t completely eliminate your stress. If you’re still struggling, try talking to a licensed mental health professional. They “can help you process your emotions and learn healthy coping skills,” Dr. Seawell says.

Adults should be getting seven hours or more a night, according to the CDC. Definitely getting less? Enter: Fatigue.

“Minimum seven hours of sleep is required for effective rejuvenation of the body and restfulness of the brain,” says Dr. Khan. Here’s the thing: Even one night of bad sleep can mess with your circadian rhythm (your sleep-wake cycle) and throw you off for a few days, she says.

How to fix it: At baseline, the solution is simply to get more sleep. But sometimes that’s easier said than done. You need to first figure out what the culprit is—stress? Netflix? Crappy sleep hygiene?—and then address it. If that still doesn't work, talk to your doctor about your options. You may need an intervention such as cognitive behavioral therapy to treat insomnia, for example.

Depression can cause a range of symptoms, and decreased energy or fatigue is definitely one of them, according to the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH). “Whenever I am screening a patient for depression, feelings of fatigue and loss of energy are one of the symptoms I always inquire about,” says Dr. Seawell.

These are the symptoms of depression to be familiar with, according to the NIMH.

Worth noting: Not everyone with depression experiences every symptom, per the NIMH. So, it’s entirely possible for you to feel tired on the regular and not even realize that it’s due to depression.

How to fix it: In this case, you need to address the underlying cause of your fatigue before you’ll feel better. Depression can be treated with psychotherapy, medication, or a combination of the two. If you suspect that your fatigue is linked to depression, though, it’s best to talk to your doctor about getting evaluated.

Your thyroid is a small, butterfly-shaped gland in the front of your neck that produces hormones that regulate how your body uses energy. When it doesn't produce enough thyroid hormone, it causes a condition known as hypothyroidism, which can mess with or slow down many of your body's functions, according to MedlinePlus.

“Thyroid hormones have receptors on essentially every organ of the human body and their deficiency can cause fatigue by excessively slowing the metabolic pathways,” explains Dr. Khan.

How to fix it: The treatment for hypothyroidism is taking medication to replace the hormone that your own thyroid can no longer make or create a sufficient amount of to keep your body functioning normally. Just know this: It may take a little while to feel better. Your doctor may need to adjust your medication until you reach the optimal level.

Just because you’re on the mend from, say, a virus doesn’t mean you should expect to bounce back energy-wise automatically. Recovery can take time. "A viral or bacterial infection can cause dehydration, generalized inflammation, and immense fatigue," says Dr. Khan.

How to fix it: First, give yourself time to recoup. Drink plenty of water and just take it easy, and you should feel less tired and more like yourself in a week or two.

Anemia is a condition in which your blood has fewer than normal red blood cells or hemoglobin, according to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI). Hemoglobin is an iron-rich protein that helps red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body. According to the NHLBI, if you have anemia, your body doesn't get enough oxygen-rich blood. So, if you have the condition, you can struggle with “fatigue and excessive tiredness,” says Dr. Khan.

How to fix it: It depends on the type of anemia you have. For some types of mild to moderate anemia, you may just need to add OTC or prescription iron supplements to your regimen. But your doctor may also suggest certain vitamins, IV therapy, or medicines that make your body produce more red blood cells, according to the NHLBI. You may also need to incorporate more iron-rich foods into your diet. Basically, you should see your doc for this one.

Gluten is a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye. In some people, gluten damages the small intestine and causes symptoms like bloating, diarrhea, constipation, gas, nausea, stomach pain, vomiting, and yep, fatigue, according to the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK). That happens to people with celiac disease.

This condition can also cause long-term digestive issues that keep you from getting the nutrients you need and, in turn, cause ongoing fatigue.

How to fix it: Celiac disease can be tricky to diagnose, but after a physical exam, your doctor may recommend a blood test and an intestinal biopsy to check for inflammation in your small intestine. If you are confirmed to have celiac disease, you’ll need to avoid foods containing gluten in the future.

This is a less likely diagnosis, but it’s still worth mentioning. MS is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the brain and spinal cord, damaging the myelin, the covering of nerve fibers, according to the National Multiple Sclerosis Society (NMSS).

Fatigue is a very common symptom in people with MS—about 80 percent of patients struggle with it, according to the NMSS. The fatigue can significantly interfere with a person’s ability to function, even if they feel good otherwise. It can result from treatable medication side effects or other factors.

How to fix it: Specific treatments can help people with MS manage fatigue, including occupational therapy to simplify tasks at home, physical therapy to learn energy-saving ways to walk and do other day-to-day tasks, a regular exercise program, sleep regulation, and psychological interventions, per the NMSS.

This is another one to add to the category of “unlikely but worth knowing.” Cancer-related fatigue is incredibly common: At least 80 percent of people diagnosed with the condition experience it, according to the American Cancer Society (ACS). While cancer treatments could be to blame, people with cancer can also feel wiped out just from the disease itself. It can disrupt almost all metabolic pathways and sabotage the body's mitochondrial energy, Dr. Khan explains.

How to fix it: First, don't freak out that you have a serious health issue. But know that getting a proper diagnosis is important and, from there, proper treatment is needed, which usually involves chemotherapy, radiation therapy, surgery, or immunotherapy. The exact course depends on what type of cancer you have and how advanced it is. That's why seeing your doctor to rule it out is key if you haven't been able to shake your tiredness for a long time.

Here's the thing: Our body needs a range of nutrients and a certain number of calories per day to run at its normal capacity. Those numbers vary for everyone. "You need to not only make sure that you're providing yourself with a sufficient amount of calories per day to function, but also you need to be providing yourself with the appropriate nutrients," says Dr. Price.

If you don't, which can add to the fatigue, Dr. Price adds, even the smallest task feels monumental. You can also become constipated, says Dr. Price, which can contribute to the fatigue.

How to fix it: Eating a well-balanced diet and making sure that you’re eating enough fruits, vegetables, and proteins s essential to combatting fatigue, says Dr. Price. With the right nutrients, your body can create the energy you need to go about your day.

You’ve heard it before, but it’s true: Caffeine is a drug. Once your body gets accustomed to it, especially if you have coffee or soda every day, you become dependent on it. While it gives you a boost, caffeine also comes with highs and lows, and that can make you feel extremely tired, says Dr. Price. “Because you're burning calories when you have caffeine, you're moving at a faster pace, and you get to your peak of exhaustion much quicker,” she explains.

If you absolutely need coffee to get through your day, that should be a warning sign. "You should not have to have coffee in order to function, and something else is going on in your life that is causing you to be extremely fatigued," notes Dr. Price.

How to fix it: Switch up how you get your caffeine and start weaning yourself off of it. It'll take some adjustment, and you might get headaches at first, but once your body no longer depends on coffee, you'll feel a lot better.

While the medical world is still trying to figure out the long-term effects of COVID-19, we do know the toll the disease has on your body is that it makes you extremely exhausted, says Dr. Price. Your body tries to recuperate when you're infected—you lose your appetite, your muscles are extremely fatigued, and your body works in overdrive.

“Your body is doing the most to get you back to your normal self and to fight off COVID, so once you're done with it, you're not just going to bounce right back to yourself," says Dr. Price. “It's also been shown that the peak symptoms of COVID can sometimes be 14 days later. People must keep in mind this isn't a short illness. There are different and great severities of it."

Long COVID usually occurs two months after a person had COVID, says Dr. Price. If, two months after contracting the novel coronavirus, you’re still feeling worn out, it could be long COVID, she says.

How to fix it: The best way to protect yourself against COVID and the long-term complications is to get vaccinated and boosted and keep practicing good hygiene. If you suspect you have long COVID, visit your primary care provider and discuss your symptoms, Dr. Price advises. They can help you figure out your next steps.

Feeling tired once in a while is pretty normal—but experiencing constant fatigue isn’t. If you’re struggling, Dr. Khan recommends seeing your doctor. They’ll likely order several tests, including a physical exam and blood work, to figure out what, if anything, is happening.

"It's never too soon to go and talk to your doctor," says Dr. Price. What you thought might be minor, the doctor might look into more. "Or maybe you started googling things and, of course, Google will tell you you're dying, so talking to your doctor can give you relief and reassurance," Dr. Price adds.

The upside: the sooner you seek help, the sooner you can get answers—and get back to your rejuvenated and energetic self.

#5093. Claude-Built Linux Exploit Targets Bug That Ubuntu Still Hasn't Patched

Claude-Built Linux Exploit Targets Bug That Ubuntu Still Hasn't Patched

Another day, another exploit from ChatGPT or Claude that gives us the chills.

Anthropic says its AI wrote a working attack that lets a stranger take full control of a Linux server over the internet, no password needed. The bug behind it, CVE-2026-98432, has been hiding in Linux since version 4.4 and scores 9.8 out of 10 for severity.

Linux runs countless servers, and Ubuntu is one of its most popular flavors. Ubuntu's own tracker still lists every version from 16.04 to 26.10 as vulnerable.

Anthropic described the attack on Oct. 27 in a research post covering five targets: Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows, and Linux. Claude wrote the Linux exploit after initial prompting, using an unreleased internal model.

The attack takes less than an hour to find a hidden spot in the computer's memory, then five more minutes to run a command with the highest level of access, known as root.

The flaw works like reading a sticky note after someone already shredded it. One part of the system throws away a piece of information while another part is still using it, per AlmaLinux. A specially crafted message that opens an internet connection can set that off.

Failing costs the attacker almost nothing. "An enabling property of this race condition is that a lost race only fails the handshake without crashing the whole system," Anthropic wrote, "so a determined attacker can retry indefinitely until they succeed."

Anthropic's version needs a server using a feature called multipath TCP, which lets one connection travel over several routes at once. Programs written in Go have switched it on by default since Go 1.24, per the Go Security Team.

But the bug is not limited to that feature. "While the demonstrated exploit requires the target system to expose an MPTCP listener, the underlying bug is not specific to MPTCP," the Go Security Team wrote.

Red Hat released fixes for RHEL 8, 9 and 10 on Sunday, including RHSA-2026:93412. Debian, SUSE, Oracle Linux and Amazon Linux have also shipped fixes, at least for some versions.

For anyone who can't update yet, Red Hat published a temporary firewall rule. It "reduces exposure to this vulnerability but cannot fully prevent it," Red Hat says in its security bulletin. A full working solution is still under development.

Anthropic's earlier Claude Mythos model helped Mozilla find 271 bugs in Firefox, as Decrypt reported in April.

Ubuntu's tracker shows fixes in progress for 22.04, 24.04, 26.04 and 26.10. Versions 20.04, 18.04 and 16.04 show only "Vulnerable," and the tracker gives no release date for any fix.

#5092. CZ calls for crypto security alliance as AI-driven attacks accelerate after Binance hack

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

Changpeng Zhao says companies need AI-based defenses and an industry alliance to share lessons and freeze stolen funds faster, in his first interview since the Oct. 29 hack.

Binance cofounder and former CEO Changpeng "CZ" Zhao said AI is accelerating cyberattacks and argued companies should invest in AI-based defenses, security personnel, and partnerships with AI security providers.

In his first public interview since the Oct. 29 hack of Binance, Zhao told the Talking Tokens podcast that the threat extends beyond individual companies to the broader crypto industry and global financial system, given crypto's connections to stablecoins, tokenized stocks, real-world assets, and traditional finance.

"The speed of hacking is going to pick up because of AI capabilities [being] so strong now. At the same time, we've got to use more AI to defend. The only way to fight a monster is to kind of become that monster."

The comments come amid a string of security incidents across the crypto industry, including a separate AI-assisted breach at blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis and a $46 million security incident at Brazilian exchange Mercado Bitcoin.

Zhao said he learned of the incident around midnight in the UAE and focused on communicating with the community while Binance's team worked to contain the attack and protect users. He attributed relatively calm market conditions and subsequent net inflows to the company's response, financial capacity and user trust. He described security incidents as preventable with sufficient effort and attention, while warning that organizations can become complacent.

Earlier Tuesday, Binance said hackers used a fake job interview to compromise an employee's computer before leveraging an internal AI tool in the attack. The exchange also said it detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threats in 2026.

Zhao called for an industry alliance to share lessons and best practices, conduct cross-audits and help freeze stolen funds more quickly. He views security as an ongoing process rather than a milestone that must be reached before adoption.

"As an industry, I encourage [...] forming some kind of industry alliance on security to help each other learn from each other's mistakes, share the best practices, cross audits, help each other freeze funds very quickly, etc."

Zhao said he had not spoken with President Donald Trump or other U.S. officials about the incident, but that Binance and the broader crypto industry would welcome government assistance. Trump has said the U.S. was "looking into it."

"What's bad for crypto on this scale has real economic impact elsewhere," Zhao said. "So you cannot just say, 'Look, this is one specific problem for one specific sector or for one specific company.' It impacts the company, impacts the industry, impacts global finance. It's all interconnected, and I think, given the size of impact, it's definitely at the national security level as well."

Zhao expressed optimism that AI could help identify software vulnerabilities and strengthen defenses, while blockchain could support faster transactions facilitated by AI.

#5091. 8 Best Hand Creams of 2026: 3-plus Years of Editor Testing and Reviews

From Joonbyrd to L’Occitane, here’s what formulas actually work.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I’ll be the first to admit it: I spend a copious amount of money on spa treatments and refining my at-home skincare routine. From my $78 Isdin sunscreen and Paula’s Choice Exfoliant to biweekly facials, my focus has always been on achieving clear, wrinkle-free skin without injections. But after chatting with double board-certified dermatologist Serena Mraz, MD, I realized that I’ve been neglecting my hands for far too long.

As a New Yorker, I take the subway several times a day for work, events, and to meet up with friends. I’m also a germaphobe and rely on hand sanitizer or harsh soap in office and restaurant bathrooms after riding the train. As a result, my hands are inevitably dry, dull, and rough. That's not exactly the look I’m going for as our beauty editor. It also doesn’t help that Dr. Mraz says cumulative sun damage, including dark spots and wrinkles, is one of the biggest culprits in showing my age. Wait, what do you mean my age didn’t pause during the pandemic? “Your skin records sun exposure like your car tallies mileage,” dermatologist Hadley King, MD, previously told me about how skincare changes in your 40s. “You can't turn back the odometer on your car, and you can't turn back sun damage from your skin."

Hand creams provide instant hydration and support the skin barrier, helping me achieve the baby-soft skin of my dreams. I’ve noticed that investing in my favorites lets me reapply less frequently and use a smaller amount of product, ultimately trimming my cost per use. It’s beauty math, ladies!

Creams, such as L'Occitane and Beau Domaine, are the thickest and most nourishing type of hand care products. Dr. Mraz is a fan of creams because they’re packed with more lipids than water, which helps deliver the best moisture. The downside is that they take longer to rub into your hands and across larger areas like your arms.

Ointments, such as Aquaphor and Vaseline, are versatile, fragrance-free moisturizers that relieve dryness without causing irritation, says dermatologist and clinical professor of dermatology Gary Goldenberg, MD. They’re made with petrolatum to keep your skin moist, which helps prevent wounds from drying out and forming a scab. These are especially useful when you have super cracked skin.

Lotions are thinner and more fluid than creams. Some are even runny, but don’t worry: the right lotions still restore moisture for instant relief and prevent dryness. Notably, our best overall pick—Joonbyrd Wonder·Land Hand Lotion—has a luxurious consistency that feels and smells like it belongs in a spa. It’s so enjoyable, I use it all over my body and notice instant hydration without leaving residue on my clothes.

The dermatologists I consulted recommend moisturizing ingredients glycerin, shea butter, and cocoa butter—they can be found in many of our suggestions, like Aquaphor and Juara.

Hyaluronic acid is another standout that acts as a moisture magnet, holding up to 1,000 times its weight in water. It’s so epic that dermatologists recently told me you can even use hyaluronic acid on your hair and scalp.

As our fragrance-obsessed beauty editor, I also factored in the scent profiles. While all of these hand creams smell good, I also highlighted the key notes that make each one stand out. To narrow the list further, I used these hand creams twice daily for five months. I adored our best overall pick so much that I used it for an entire month straight before even writing this story because it’s genuinely that good.

I didn’t want the hand cream application to feel like a mundane process. To help you actually finish your next tube of hand cream, I evaluated each contender’s sensory experience. This final list includes a mix of affordable, mid-range, and splurge-worthy picks that provide varying levels of hydration and other cosmetic-enhancing benefits like lightening age spots.

Ready to make dry hands a thing of the past? Look no further than these eight expert-approved hand creams worthy of a spot in your routine.

As our beauty editor, I’m constantly searching for the next big thing. My new undisputed no. 1 hand cream hails from the U.K. and it quickly became my all-time favorite recommendation. My picky, scent-averse mom also found the sophisticated warm and sweet gourmand notes appealing.

Aroma aside, the formulation and ingredient list are on point. The fast-absorbing, nourishing lotion is made with all my favorite heavy hitters: ceramides, amino acids, and niacinamide. They’re basically a trifecta of skincare goodness that repair my skin barrier and hydrate.

Joonbyrd says this hand lotion moisturizes for up to 48 hours. However, I’m a frequent handwasher, so I can’t speak to going two full days without soap and water on my skin. Personally, I noticed my hands felt softer after a week of consistent reapplication, and I can use this lotion twice daily afterward.

I initially tested it for one month straight before comparing it to other picks. (More on that shortly!) Since then, I’ve been reaching for it almost daily for a year. It offers long-lasting hydration and skin barrier support. Joonbyrd is so effective at leaving my skin softer and more supple that even acquaintances have noticed how soft my hands feel.

To ensure others received a fair assessment during the second month of my testing process, I evaluated how Joonbyrd compared with other options.

Joonbyrd wins over the French staple, as it’s lighter and features a modern formula that strengthens the skin barrier. L’Occitane remains a beauty classic, but if you want something new that you can apply all over your body, opt for Joonbyrd.

Go with the latter if you’re a price-conscious shopper or just super sensitive to scents. Hey, it happens to me during the spring and summer, so I totally get it! Joonbyrd is luxurious—the pretty packaging elevates my vanity setup, and the green, textured exterior helps prevent it from rolling off my table.

Joonbyrd is a non-sticky lotion that absorbs quickly, leaving no pesky residue on my belongings. It’s your best bet when your hands require barrier support and nourishment. On the flip side, Aquaphor feels heavy compared to Joonbyrd’s formulation, but not as greasy as Vaseline. (More on that soon—promise!)

Here’s where things get tougher. HomeCourt offers an aspirational, Insta-famous brand vibe, but with hydrating ingredients that enhance my skin. I also like HomeCourt partially because it offers five fragrances ranging from floral to aromatic and citrus. It provides just enough hydration after washing my dishes or hands. Woo! But if I could only own one hand cream, I’d opt for Joonbyrd since it’s cosmetically elegant and effective. FWIW, HomeCourt makes a body care collection if you prefer. I’m also so obsessed with the 2026 Skincare Award-winning Exfoliating Hand Soap.

Both hand creams provide ample skin-replenishing goodness. While the fragrance-free Nécessaire Hand Cream is helpful for anyone with a sensitive nose and skin, I do miss having access to the line’s signature scents at my disposal.

Overall, Joonbyrd is the best hand cream to beat in 2026. I’ll continue using this nourishing lotion for its standout ingredients, luxurious feeling, and impressive short- and long-term performance. Plus, the packaging is pretty and adds a fun, feminine touch to my vanity. The container has a nice weight and features a lightly cushioned textured green exterior to help prevent accidental slippage.

CeraVe makes a strong case that you don’t have to splurge to enjoy a solid hand cream. But at just $10 a tube, it’s by far the most affordable recommendation, making it a major win in my book. Pick this hand cream if you’re shopping on a budget and don’t want to skimp on moisture and barrier repair.

Arguably the most famous hand cream of the bunch, L'Occitane's non-greasy formula has earned plenty of love from our beauty team. We previously featured this exact product in our at-home manicure tutorial and highlighted the brand in our Skincare Awards and guides to the best spa-worthy bodycare products.

So what makes it so iconic? L’Occitane is made with gentle, effective ingredients, such as 20 percent organic shea butter, glycerin, and skin-plumping omegas. The consistency is thick enough to keep my hands hydrated overnight, yet it absorbs relatively fast enough that it won't leave a trail on my keyboard.Before I wrote about beauty for nine years, I was a tad excessive with products. The trick is that less is truly more with this South of France staple, and find the ideal amount for you, which varies based on your environment and how active you’ve been with your hands. Since Courteney Cox launched Homecourt in 2022, the brand’s stylish design and hydrating formula elevate handcare into a sensory experience that I always look forward to using. While I’m all in on her All-Purpose Spray, it’s her splurge-worthy Hand Wash and Hand Cream that seal the deal for me.

Aquaphor and Vaseline are similar drugstore staples—they both use petroleum to lock in moisture and repair the skin barrier. It’s made with a mineral oil called paraffinum liquidum and a wax called ceresin. There’s also soothing bisabolol, and a blend of hydrating glycerin, lanolin, and panthenol.

Though Juara doesn't make any specific eczema safety certifications, Dr. Ruth doesn’t mind it for her patients with that skin condition. TBH, my eczema flares up during the winter and seasonal transitions, but this nourishing cream hasn’t caused any sensitivity issues.

Embryolisse is a French pharmacy staple trusted by our beauty team and the lead makeup artist on Emily in Paris. Most know Lait-Crème Concentré as a face moisturizer and makeup primer—it leaves my skin dewy even after using retinol—but it functions six ways, including as a hand cream. Wait, what? Mhmmm, I apply a small pea-sized amount of Lait-Crème Concentré to hydrate my hands without feeling greasy or sticky. Chock-full of shea butter and soothing aloe vera, my hands look visibly hydrated and luminous. I rub it into my hands and get back to typing on my laptop or phone within a minute.

With holiday travel coming up, carry-on space is limited and valuable. Think of Lait-Crème Concentré as the Swiss Army knife of skincare. It works as a moisturizing face mask, after-sun treatment, shaving cream, and cleansing milk—yup, just add a little water for a hydrating wash. This lightweight cream also helps minimize my retinol-related flaking and redness.TBH, I like pretty much everything about this multipurpose hand cream. The only con is that the larger size is currently out of stock on Amazon. Still, at just $19 for an icon from the French pharmacy, you can’t go wrong, especially since you won’t deal with VAT refunds at CDG Airport in Paris.

#5089. ‘Scromiting’ and Other Super Scary Symptoms of Taking High-THC Weed

Yes, that’s vomiting and screaming at the same time.

In November 1996, California became the first state to legalize medical cannabis. (Many) politics and (some) physicians promised us breakthroughs in better health. Thirty years later, how are we really doing? Men’s Health decided to find out in this special report package. Read more here.

HIGH-CONCENTRATION SYNTHETIC THC products are producing wild reactions in some people. Kevin Gray, MD, a practicing physician and director of addiction sciences at Medical University of South Carolina, helps break them down.

“You experience hallucinations, paranoia, delusions,” says Dr. Gray. “It’s become undeniable looking at the association between teen cannabis use and psychosis that if somebody has some kind of already innate risk for developing a psychotic disorder, there’s something about use of cannabis during this stage of development that [may trigger the onset of] a lifelong disorder.” (The risk of someone developing the condition is less than 1 percent.)

“Paranoia is a symptom of psychosis. Instead of feeling the usual sort of high and calming feeling with cannabis, people feel more detached and more suspicious. Sometimes there will be a very high concentration or some unusual strain that may be more likely to lead to paranoia. The effect can be intense, but it’s transient and wears off with time.”

That’s screaming and vomiting at the same time. “Cyclic vomiting, cannabis-related emesis—I don’t see it that often among my clients, but it happens,” says Dr. Gray. “THC can reduce nausea, but there’s something about the interaction between THC and the systems that control our nausea that goes haywire in some people. We don’t know even how to treat it symptomatically, other than taking showers.” So if you totally misread a gummy label, just call 911—no judgment.

There’s so much more going on in the world of weed and health. Read more here.

#5088. Mystery $106 Million Crypto Theft Hits EU Entity Days After Binance Hack

Mystery $106 Million Crypto Theft Hits EU Entity Days After Binance Hack

Another nine-figure theft has hit crypto, just days after the biggest heist in the industry’s history.

An unnamed entity in the European Union is suspected of losing more than $106 million from several of its accounts on centralized exchanges on Sunday, pseudonymous onchain investigator ZachXBT said Monday in a post to his Telegram channel.

The funds were withdrawn as USDC and USDT stablecoins by what he called an “illicit actor.”

ZachXBT published 11 Ethereum addresses tied to the theft.

Instant exchanges let users quickly swap one cryptocurrency for another, often with little identity verification, while Monero hides senders, receivers and amounts, making it a popular tool for obscuring stolen funds.

Swapping out of USDC and USDT also matters because the companies behind those stablecoins can freeze them.

ZachXBT said the culprit remains unidentified, but that he could say “with a high degree of confidence” that it isn’t Lazarus Group, citing multiple laundering indicators. Lazarus is the umbrella name often used for North Korea’s state-backed hackers. ZachXBT didn’t name the victim.

That sets the theft apart from the record-setting $6.4 billion Binance hack, which the FBI has attributed to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group.

In that case, stablecoin issuers moved within minutes. Tether froze stolen USDT on Ethereum in 37 minutes, and Circle froze all $823 million in stolen USDC, helping lock up about 44% of the haul, according to blockchain analytics firm Elliptic.

North Korea’s launderers have since spread the remaining funds across about 12,000 wallets. It’s unclear whether any funds in the EU case have been frozen.

The incident adds to an already unprecedented week for crypto security. Beyond the record-breaking Binance hack, Brazilian exchange Mercado Bitcoin just today reported halting withdrawals after a $40 million hack of its own. Likewise today, BTCPay Server told merchants to switch off their servers amid reports of hot wallet attacks.

#5087. SEC division views Canton Coin as digital commodity in no-action letter

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

a16z partner Miles Jennings welcomed the SEC staff's position, arguing it could signal a broader regulatory path for blockchain network tokens.

The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission's Division of Corporation Finance said it views Canton Coin (CC) as a digital commodity and will not recommend enforcement action over its programmatic issuance under certain conditions.

In a no-action letter published Tuesday, the division said Canton Coin derives its value from the programmatic operation of the Canton Network and supply-and-demand dynamics, rather than expectations of profit from the managerial efforts of others. It also cited the network's lack of a central party.

"Based on the facts presented, the Division will not recommend enforcement action to the Commission if, in reliance on your opinion as counsel, Canton Coin is minted programmatically by Super Validators, Validators and application providers, in the manner and under the circumstances described in your letter, without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act or Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act," Deputy Chief Counsel Jonathan Ingram wrote.

The letter reflects the Division of Corporation Finance's enforcement position based on the specific facts and representations submitted by Canton and does not express a legal conclusion on the issues presented, including whether Canton Coin is a security.

In May, 21Shares became the first U.S. ETF issuer to offer direct exposure to CC, the network's native utility token.

In June, Digital Asset raised $355 million in a funding round led by Andreessen Horowitz's a16z crypto fund to expand the Canton ecosystem and accelerate institutional adoption of its blockchain infrastructure.

a16z partner Miles Jennings welcomed the SEC staff's position, arguing it could signal a broader regulatory path for blockchain network tokens.

"Incredible. @CantonNetwork just received no action relief from the SEC for its network token," Jennings wrote Tuesday on X. "The @SECGov's token taxonomy from March and follow up FAQs have now created a clear pathway out of securities laws—Network tokens are digital commodities."

#5085. 30 Years of Legal Weed: Has It Made Us Any Healthier?

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

The very highs and bizarre lows of America on medicinal marijuana.

EARLIER THIS YEAR, during a brief and mercifully abandoned period when I was considering doing stand-up as a hobby, I went to a comedy show in downtown Austin. I was legitimately shocked to find, as part of the two-drink minimum bill of fare, the option for several different flavors of $5 THC seltzers. This wasn’t “take a pull off your vape or smoke a roach in the alley before the show” territory. No, marijuana drinks were on the menu.

In the past few years, my only social activities have been poker, competitive trivia, and going to the movies, all activities people do stoned, but not activities where you can literally order drugs from the bar alongside your chicken wings. The comedy club, on the other hand, considered marijuana products as a profit center.

This was one of those lightly attended weeknight shows where the comedians banter with the audience because they haven’t prepared much material. So, during a Q&A, I brought up the fact that there were THC sodas available to order, in laminate. “Sir, this is 2026,” the host said.

This is where we are now, a full three decades after California legalized medical weed. But is that good for us?

As I write this, it’s been eight-and-a-half years since I quit marijuana, a drug that at one point made pretty much anything—listening to music, shopping for groceries, cleaning the house—fun for me.

But really, I’ve been sober since I stopped using THC, since I was hardly just smoking there at the end. I was vaping, eating, drinking, dabbing, and otherwise gorging myself on what has become an extremely potent, psychosis-inducing drug. And I wasn’t having fun.

My breaking point, which I recounted in my 2020 memoir Pothead, came at Game 2 of the 2017 World Series at Dodger Stadium, where I was so wasted on weed that I had a screaming meltdown in front of security when I found out the ticket I’d bought was fraudulent.

It was a low point, a bottom so deep and so pathetic that I should have quit right there. But I went on for another three weeks before I finally crawled to a Marijuana Anonymous meeting and asked for help.

Now, nearly a decade later, I’ve emerged from my cocoon to find that THC is everywhere. I live in a state where it’s still technically illegal, but you can find some sort of THC variant in most convenience stores and in most bars and nightclubs.

My friend is an attorney who represents the Texas Alcoholic Beverage Commission. He says his client is in a near panic. Sales are down for every beverage except for nonalcoholic mixers and those THC seltzers. THC is the beer, wine, and vodka of the present day, combined.

And so we find ourselves in a bizarre situation where people are drinking way less alcohol because it’s unhealthy for you, but they are instead ingesting THC products—either through soda, gummies, or any number of other concoctions—from unknown manufacturers, with unknown formulas and malleable dosages.

They’re also vaping, which emerging research is showing is kind of awful for our lungs. A University of Michigan study recently showed that teens who vaped cannabis were twice as likely to experience respiratory symptoms like “wheezing or whistling” in the chest than those who vaped nicotine or smoked traditional cigarettes.

Unlike traditional marijuana, this stuff isn’t “from the earth.” Who knows where it’s really from—or where it’s going?

When I quit weed in 2017, and somewhat loudly and publicly announced myself as an addict, I got the requisite amount of sympathy, but also a tremendous amount of pushback. Marijuana isn’t dangerous, people said. It isn’t addictive. It’s actually good for you.

In 2016, Gavin Newsom, then California’s lieutenant governor, spearheaded the legalization push for recreational marijuana. Cannabis sales have produced more than $8 billion in tax revenue for California since retail sales began in 2018, with a decent proportion of that funneled into teen substance-abuse prevention programs. But the state has also seen an increase in children suffering from cannabis poisoning.

It’s been a massive shift, moving from medically administered weed for veterans and cancer patients to powerful THC beverages you can buy at your bodega.

Legalization has created a new frontier of intoxicants without a centralized warning system for users. Data from a 2025 national study of U.S. adults stated that 15 percent of respondents reported daily or near-daily cannabis use.

Among those daily users, 18 percent reported experiencing symptoms consistent with cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome, a disorder characterized by cyclic, severe nausea, intractable vomiting, and gut pain alleviated temporarily by hot baths or showers.

This translates to an estimated 7.2 million people in the United States alone, many of them teenagers, experiencing these symptoms. That number is probably vastly underestimated, given that fewer than 12 percent of sufferers have received a formal diagnosis.

Welcome to the darker side of legalized weed, a world of cannabis-induced psychosis, “scromiting” (yes, screaming while vomiting), and concoctions like “shatter” or “wax,” which contain up to 90 percent THC, as opposed to the 3 to 5 percent in joints from previous decades.

So I find myself in a somewhat odd situation. I was a relatively early victim of modern weed’s potency, as well as a relatively early unadopter, and a very early voice in the wilderness warning the world that marijuana might not be the answer to all our health concerns. But now I find myself, like a patient waking up from a long coma, in a world where THC is as prevalent as, and cheaper than, whiskey. Yet still, I find myself thinking it should be legal. So which is it? Maybe we still don’t have enough data.

Thirty years since the start of legalization might feel like a long time, but it’s really not. In terms of scientific analysis, we’re still in relatively undiscovered country. If you’re suffering from chronic pain, or dying of cancer, marijuana is a healthier option than, say, oxycodone. But for the rest of us? No one really knows.

The only thing I can be truly sure of is that it’s no longer for me.

#5082. Bitcoin Firm Strive Climbs Up the Treasury Ranks With Another Big Buy

Bitcoin Firm Strive Climbs Up the Treasury Ranks With Another Big Buy

Strive, the Dallas-based company co-founded by Vivek Ramaswamy, now holds 43,124 Bitcoin after buying 124 BTC more last week. That stash is now worth roughly $3.3 billion, and good for about 0.2% of the 21 million coins that will ever exist.

That leaves it fourth among publicly traded companies, 390 coins behind Twenty One Capital (which holds 43,514 BTC) and 876 BTC behind Metaplanet (which holds 44,000 BTC), according to Bitcoin Treasuries data.

At Bitcoin’s price of about $77,000, those gaps are worth roughly $30 million and $67 million, respectively.

Strive is a Bitcoin treasury company—a publicly listed firm that keeps Bitcoin on its balance sheet, so anyone with a brokerage account can get exposure by buying its stock. Michael Saylor’s Strategy popularized the playbook back in 2020, and several other companies followed suit, including Strive.

Its coins cost an average of $87,785 each, or $3.8 billion in total, against a market value of $3.5 billion on Oct. 23, per its prospectus. Bitcoin has slipped since, so the pile is now worth a bit less than Strive paid for it.

The latest purchase covers Oct. 24 through Oct. 30 and was disclosed today in an SEC filing, the report US-listed companies must submit when something material happens. Strive paid about $10 million, an average of $80,526 per Bitcoin including fees, CEO Matt Cole said on X.

Strive acquired 124 $BTC for $10M at an average cost of $80,526 per bitcoin, bringing total holdings to ₿43,124.⁰⁰- Existing cash funded most purchases⁰- SATS ATM used for first time, representing 100% of weekly ATM proceeds⁰- Amplification Ratio: 62.7%⁰⁰$ASST $SATA $SATS pic.twitter.com/rFrS6y4AVc

— Matt Cole (@ColeMacro) November 2, 2026

Most of the money came from existing cash, which fell from $504.4 million to $490.4 million over the week. Strive also raised money for the first time by selling shares of a new security called SATS on the open market, Cole said, and that made up all of the week’s fundraising. It still holds 505,000 shares of Strategy’s preferred stock, known as STRC, worth about $50 million.

SATS is a preferred stock—a type of share that pays a fixed dividend before common shareholders see anything. Strive sold 7 million of them at $90 each in an October offering that raised about $630 million, and they carry a 15% annual dividend on a $100 stated value, paid every business day from Nov. 9.

On Oct. 26, Strive opened an at-the-market program—a way to sell new shares in small batches at the going price—for up to $1 billion more SATS. The prospectus says Strive expects to pay the dividends mainly by raising more capital, including selling more shares. The company has set aside 18 months of dividends in a reserve and reported no debt as of Oct. 23.

Strive’s amplification ratio, the preferred stock and debt it carries measured against the value of its Bitcoin, stood at 62.7%, or about $62.70 of obligations for every $100 of Bitcoin.

The company’s CEO has said ending 2026 as the second-largest public Bitcoin holder is possible. “I wouldn’t say that’s my base case,” Cole said on the One Chair podcast in September, “but I would say it’s in the possible set of cards.”

Saylor’s Strategy holds 849,327 Bitcoin, nearly 20 times Strive’s pile.

Twenty One Capital still holds the same 43,514 Bitcoin it had when co-founder Jack Mallers stepped down as CEO in July. His exit came as a plan by Tether to merge three Bitcoin businesses collapsed. The stock had fallen more than 80% from its highs, and his successor, Raphael Zagury, has said Twenty One should be judged on cash flow and capital discipline.

Metaplanet, a Tokyo-listed company that pivoted from hotels to Bitcoin in 2024, holds 44,000 Bitcoin after overtaking mining firm MARA in April. It has a stated goal of 100,000 by the end of 2026.

At last week’s pace of 124 Bitcoin, Strive would pass Twenty One in four weeks and Metaplanet in eight, assuming neither company buys more.

#5081. Strategy spends triple its weekly Bitcoin outlay on STRC buybacks

Strategy spent $208.2 million buying back STRC preferred shares and $65.5 million on Bitcoin, while allocating $98.5 million to its USD Cash balance.

Michael Saylor’s Strategy spent more than three times as much buying back its STRC preferred shares as it did acquiring Bitcoin last week.

Strategy repurchased $208.2 million in STRC and spent about $65.5 million buying 811 Bitcoin (BTC) at an average price of $80,846, according to a Monday 8-K filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Strategy sold about 1.18 million MSTR shares for net proceeds of $164 million. About $65.5 million funded its Bitcoin acquisition, while the remaining $98.5 million was allocated to the company’s USD Cash balance, according to the filing. The company held $132.7 million in USD Cash and $4.79 billion in its separate US dollar reserve as of Sunday.

The latest purchases followed about $664 million in STRC buybacks between Oct. 1 and Oct. 25, compared with about $72 million in Bitcoin acquisitions over that period.

Strategy’s STRC preferred stock rose 0.1% in pre-market trading on Monday, to $99.22, or about 0.8% below its $100 target price, according to Yahoo Finance. Strategy’s policy is not to issue new STRC shares below $100, limiting that source of funding while the stock trades below its target.

Another Bitcoin treasury company, Japan’s Metaplanet, reported buybacks of its common shares on Monday. It spent about 25.27 billion yen ($160 million) to buy back 96.45 million shares between Oct. 14 and Saturday, representing roughly 7.1% of its issued shares.

Fleece is a soft, synthetic fabric usually made from a polyester blend, often mixed with spandex, nylon, or cotton. Designed to mimic wool's insulating properties, fleece is lighter, more breathable, and dries faster, making it ideal for staying warm. Plus, fleece wicks away moisture and dries quickly, keeping you cozy even if you’re caught in rain or snow. Think of it like wearing a warm hug on a cold day.

When it comes to fleece leggings, the fabric blend is key. Most leggings are made from a mix of polyester and spandex, which delivers the perfect blend of warmth, stretch, and comfort. We’ll give you a quick breakdown of why these materials are key here:

Polyester traps heat, making it an ideal blend for staying warm without bulk. Compared to natural fibers like cotton, polyester dries quickly. WH editors love wearing polyester-fleece leggings on long walks since they stay warm without making you feel sweaty. It’s super lightweight yet strong, meaning you won’t feel like the material is clinging to your body. Polyester also helps leggings retain their shape over time, so stretching, sagging, and pilling are likely a thing of the past.

Nylon is a popular material in fleece leggings because of its strength, flexibility, and smooth texture. It resists wear and tear, which helps keep leggings looking brand new after every wash. Nylon also offers water resistance, which is key for outdoor activities in light rain or snow.

Spandex (also known as elastane or Lycra) is the go-to fabric for stretch and flexibility. It fits snugly and moves with you, giving you maximum comfort during high-impact activities like yoga, running, and dance. While it’s not as durable on its own, spandex is often blended with other fabrics (like nylon or polyester) to create leggings that are both stretchy and long-lasting.

Here’s the thing: Fleece leggings with thicker fabric may feel more restrictive than traditional leggings, so if you plan to wear them for high-impact activities, opting for a bigger size might be best. Look for four-way stretch fabrics like spandex for flexibility and comfort. If you're between sizes, choose based on your desired fit—size down for a sculpted look (read: tighter) or up for a relaxed, lounge-friendly feel.

Fleece leggings are perfect for workouts, offering warmth and insulation while keeping the stretch and comfort you need for full range of motion. “The leggings should have a good amount of stretch while fitting snugly, and maintaining their shape throughout the day,” says fashion designer Kadeem Alphanso Fyffe. Look for features like a wide, high-rise waistband for a secure fit.

As writers who've tried more than our fair share of leggings, we know what it takes to make a great pair. To earn a place on this list, these fleece leggings had to meet strict criteria. We analyzed everything from fabric quality and warmth to stretch, fit, and breathability. Were they soft and supportive? Did they hold their shape after multiple washes? #5078. Animoca Brands clears final hurdle for Abu Dhabi fund management

The former mobile games company is building out its fund management business in Abu Dhabi as it targets institutional demand for stablecoins and tokenized assets.

Animoca Brands said Monday it had secured approval to manage investment funds for non-retail clients in Abu Dhabi, expanding the asset management business of a company that began in mobile games before moving into blockchain gaming and venture investing.

The authorization, granted to subsidiary Animoca Asset Management (AD) Limited by Abu Dhabi Global Market’s Financial Services Regulatory Authority (FSRA), allows it to oversee funds that pool money from professional investors rather than the general public.

The approval announced Monday took effect on Oct. 13, bringing a process that began with in-principle approval in November 2025 to completion. In the intervening months, Animoca also secured a Dubai license in February to provide virtual asset brokerage and investment management services to institutional and qualified investors.

Animoca Brands was spun off from mobile game developer Animoca in 2014, initially developing and publishing games based on licensed brands alongside original titles. It shifted its focus toward blockchain in 2018 and built an investment portfolio that included OpenSea, Dapper Labs and Axie Infinity developer Sky Mavis.

In a September investor update, the company described a broader transition from a digital asset and Web3 operator into a regulated financial services institution operating across multiple jurisdictions, amid a broader push by crypto-native companies into traditional financial services. Under that strategy, digital assets are taking on a more institutional role in its business, with a focus on stablecoins, real-world asset tokenization and treasury management.

#5076. This Is Your Brain on Weed. It’s Actually Kind of Amazing.

In November 1996, California became the first state to legalize medical cannabis. (Many) politics and (some) physicians promised us breakthroughs in better health. Thirty years later, how are we really doing? Men’s Health decided to find out in this special report package. Read more here.

WHEN YOU USE weed, your brain kind of goes all over the place. You likely know about how marijuana can chill you out, make you forget yourself, and induce the munchies. But there are other fascinating ways that the drug can alter your mind.

When THC binds to receptors in your hippocampus, the compound disrupts signals and impairs memory. That’s why you may forget what you were saying mid-sentence or where you put your keys when stoned.

THC also binds to receptors in the amygdala, which can help you feel chill when high—and paranoid or anxious when you’re too high.

The back of the brain, the cerebellum, is important for balance, motor skills, and time perception. When THC gets involved, you might feel clumsier and as if time is slowing.

THC disrupts the prefrontal cortex, which oversees critical thinking, problem-solving, and processing information from your senses. As a result, you’re going to find it harder to multitask, feel more impulsive, and zone out.

THC also stimulates the release of feel-good dopamine in the nucleus accumbens. If you’re a chronic, heavy user, cannabis can dull dopamine response and potentially rewire circuitry within the nucleus accumbens, making you more susceptible to addiction.

Your prefrontal cortex and limbic system contribute to imaginative ideas. THC can bind to receptors in these regions and may reduce self-critical noise, allowing for greater free expression.

Scientists believe that the anterior cingulate cortex is central to the perception of pain, and THC seems to dampen its ability—in a good way.

There’s so much more going on in the world of weed and health. Read more here.

#5075. Mercado Bitcoin wallets show post-hack transfers after $46M theft

Brazil’s exchange Mercado Bitcoin paused deposits and withdrawals after a security breach, saying customer funds and data were safe.

Mercado Bitcoin, one of Brazil’s largest cryptocurrency exchanges, confirmed a security incident on Monday that blockchain analysts estimated drained more than $46 million from its wallets. Despite the company’s announcement that it had suspended deposits and withdrawals, addresses associated with the incident continued to receive funds for hours afterward.

Senior security engineer at Certik, Dickson Wu, published an initial post-mortem of the incident, saying the attackers “picked at eight small chains for four hours,” including Base, Optimism and Arbitrum. The attack then moved to the company’s main hot wallets before transferring tiny amounts of Ether (ETH) from 27,160 different addresses.

“So whoever did this can also move money out of MB’s customer deposit addresses,” he wrote.

Security firms have stated the hack was carried out through standard transfers rather than a smart contract exploit. Mercado Bitcoin said the breach would have no financial impact on customers.

According to Wu, hours after Mercado Bitcoin announced a temporary suspension of deposits and withdrawals, funds continued to move out of addresses tied to the breach, followed by thousands of small ETH transfers into a single address.

A spokesperson for Mercado Bitcoin told Cointelegraph that customers had suffered no losses and no data had been leaked, but the company did not respond to requests for comment on the continued transfers. A data breach could also trigger notification requirements to Brazil’s data protection authority.

The hack has not yet been attributed to an organized group and remains under investigation.

Of the stolen funds, by 4:42 pm UTC approximately $6.2 million had been frozen by stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle. About $20 million had been transferred into newly created wallets, while over $20 million remained in associated addresses identified by Mercado Bitcoin, including all 106 BTC.

Mercado Bitcoin had 4.5 million users as of July, when stablecoin issuer Tether announced a $20 million investment to support its expansion in tokenization, payments and credit. Another Tether-backed exchange in Latin America, Chile’s Orionx, announced its closure in September after a forensic audit found that more than $7 million in customer assets had moved to wallets outside its control.

The incident comes days after Binance reported a $6.3 billion hack targeting its hot wallets on Thursday. The exchange suspended deposits and withdrawals and pledged to cover customer losses. Binance began resuming withdrawals on Sunday, saying it had replenished 95% of the stolen assets.
